lead: A photodiode turns light into current at a fixed rate. Quantum efficiency η counts how many of the arriving photons give a collected electron; responsivity R gives the current in amperes for each watt of light. Together they connect the optical power in a fiber to the electrical signal a receiver sees, so a link designer can say "1 µW in gives about 0.5 µA out". Only a few universities teach this as a topic of its own; most fold it into the photodiode chapter.
prereq: You need photon energy and the bandgap from the chapter on optical sources: E = hν = hc/λ and λ = 1.24/E<sub>g</sub>.

sections.h3: Photon energy and the photon rate

blocks.text: A photon of wavelength λ carries energy E = hν = hc/λ. Here h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s is Planck's constant, ν is the optical frequency in hertz, c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s is the speed of light and λ is in metres. At λ = 0.85 µm, E = 2.34 × 10⁻¹⁹ J; at 1.55 µm, E = 1.28 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. A longer wavelength means a weaker photon.

An optical power of P watts is a stream of photons. Each second P/E photons arrive. So 1 µW at 0.85 µm is about 4.3 × 10¹² photons per second, and 1 µW at 1.55 µm is about 7.8 × 10¹² photons per second, because each photon at 1.55 µm carries less energy.

sections.h3: Quantum efficiency and the cutoff wavelength

blocks.text: η = (electrons collected per second) ÷ (photons arriving per second)
η is a pure ratio with no units, between 0 and 1. A good PIN photodiode has η of about 0.7 to 0.9.

Photons are lost in three ways. Some are reflected at the surface before they enter the semiconductor (an antireflection coating keeps this to a few percent). Some pass through the absorbing layer without being absorbed. Some create electron–hole pairs that recombine before the junction field collects them. Each loss lowers η.

A photon is absorbed only if its energy is at least the bandgap E<sub>g</sub>. So every material has a cutoff wavelength λ<sub>c</sub> = 1.24/E<sub>g</sub> (λ<sub>c</sub> in µm, E<sub>g</sub> in eV). Beyond λ<sub>c</sub> the material is transparent and η = 0. In a real diode η starts to fall a little before λ<sub>c</sub>, because absorption grows weak near the band edge. The cutoff is a property of the material, not of the circuit.
This is why silicon cannot be used in the 1.3 µm and 1.55 µm fiber windows: its cutoff is 1.11 µm.
Each collected electron carries charge q = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. The primary photocurrent I<sub>p</sub> is q times the number of electrons collected per second, which is η times the photon rate P/(hν).

blocks.where: I<sub>p</sub> is the photocurrent in A and P the optical power falling on the diode in W.
R is the responsivity in A/W. In the last form λ is in micrometres: 1.24 µm·V is hc/q worked out.

blocks.text: R grows in proportion to λ for a fixed η, because at a longer wavelength one watt holds more photons. Since η ≤ 1, a photodiode without gain has R ≤ λ/1.24: about 0.69 A/W at 0.85 µm, 1.05 A/W at 1.3 µm and 1.25 A/W at 1.55 µm. This ceiling holds for the primary current of a PN or PIN diode. An avalanche photodiode multiplies the primary current by its gain M, so its measured responsivity MR can be many times the ceiling; the primary R inside it still obeys R ≤ λ/1.24.

Some syllabi ask for quantum efficiency and responsivity as two separate definitions; others ask for the derivation of R = ηqλ/(hc). The junction that collects the carriers is the subject of PN and PIN photodiodes, and gain is the subject of Avalanche photodiodes.

examples.question: A silicon PIN photodiode has η = 0.8 at λ = 0.85 µm and receives P = 1 µW. Find the photon arrival rate, the collected electron rate, the photocurrent and the responsivity. Take h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s, c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s and q = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
steps: Photon rate: N<sub>p</sub> = P/E = (1 × 10⁻⁶ W)/(2.339 × 10⁻¹⁹ J) = 4.28 × 10¹² photons per second.
Collected electron rate: N<sub>e</sub> = ηN<sub>p</sub> = 0.8 × 4.28 × 10¹² = 3.42 × 10¹² electrons per second.
Responsivity: R = I<sub>p</sub>/P = 0.548 µA/1 µW = 0.548 A/W. Check with the shortcut: R = ηλ/1.24 = 0.8 × 0.85/1.24 = 0.548 A/W. The two routes agree.
Compare with the ceiling at 0.85 µm: λ/1.24 = 0.685 A/W, and 0.548/0.685 = 0.8 = η, as it must be.
examples.answer: N<sub>p</sub> = 4.28 × 10¹² s⁻¹, N<sub>e</sub> = 3.42 × 10¹² s⁻¹, I<sub>p</sub> = 0.548 µA and R = 0.548 A/W.

examples.question: An InGaAs photodiode gives 0.90 µA when 1.0 µW of 1.55 µm light falls on it. Find its responsivity and quantum efficiency. Would the same diode respond at 1.70 µm? (E<sub>g</sub> of InGaAs = 0.75 eV.)
steps: Responsivity: R = I<sub>p</sub>/P = 0.90 µA/1.0 µW = 0.90 A/W.
Quantum efficiency: η = 1.24R/λ = 1.24 × 0.90/1.55 = 0.72. So 72 % of the photons give a collected electron.
Check by counting: photons per second = P/E = 1 × 10⁻⁶/1.282 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 7.80 × 10¹²; electrons per second = I<sub>p</sub>/q = 0.90 × 10⁻⁶/1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 5.62 × 10¹²; ratio 5.62/7.80 = 0.72.
Cutoff: λ<sub>c</sub> = 1.24/0.75 = 1.65 µm. At 1.70 µm the photon energy is 1.24/1.70 = 0.73 eV, below the bandgap, so the light is not absorbed and R = 0.
examples.answer: R = 0.90 A/W and η = 0.72; at 1.70 µm the diode does not respond, because 1.70 µm is beyond its 1.65 µm cutoff.

traps: Putting λ in metres into R = ηλ/1.24. The 1.24 shortcut needs λ in micrometres; with λ in metres use R = ηqλ/(hc).
Mixing up the units: η has no units, R is in A/W. "η = 0.8 A/W" loses the mark.
Saying no detector can ever show R above λ/1.24. The ceiling is for the primary current; an APD with gain M shows MR, which can be far above it.
Taking η = 1 by default. Surface reflection, light that passes through, and recombination all make η less than 1.
Using R = ηλ/1.24 past the cutoff wavelength. Beyond λ<sub>c</sub> = 1.24/E<sub>g</sub> the material does not absorb, so R = 0, not a larger value.

quiz.a: η = electrons collected per second ÷ photons arriving per second. It is a pure ratio with no units.

quiz.q: Write the responsivity formula when λ is in micrometres.
Why does η have no units while R has the unit A/W?
quiz.a: η counts particles per particle. R is current per optical power: coulombs per second per watt, which is A/W.

quiz.q: A detector has η = 0.9 at λ = 1.3 µm and receives P = 10 µW. Find R and I<sub>p</sub>.
At λ = 1.55 µm the received power is 2 µW. Find the photon arrival rate.
quiz.a: E = hc/λ = 1.282 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Rate = P/E = 2 × 10⁻⁶/1.282 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 1.56 × 10¹³ photons per second.

quiz.q: Germanium has E<sub>g</sub> = 0.66 eV. Can a germanium photodiode detect 1.55 µm light? Can silicon (E<sub>g</sub> = 1.12 eV)?
quiz.a: Ge: λ<sub>c</sub> = 1.24/0.66 = 1.88 µm, longer than 1.55 µm, so yes. Si: λ<sub>c</sub> = 1.24/1.12 = 1.11 µm, shorter than 1.55 µm, so no.

quiz.q: Why is R = λ/1.24 an upper bound for a PIN photodiode, and why does an APD not obey it?
quiz.a: Each photon gives at most one collected electron, so η = 1 is the best case and then R = qλ/(hc) = λ/1.24. An APD multiplies each primary electron by its gain M, so its output current per watt is MR, which is not limited by one electron per photon.

quiz.q: Why does R fall to zero beyond the cutoff wavelength instead of continuing to rise with λ?
quiz.a: R = ηλ/1.24 rises with λ only while η stays constant. Beyond λ<sub>c</sub> the photon energy is below the bandgap, absorption stops and η drops to zero, so R = 0.

beyond: Not for the exam. Waveguide photodetectors in silicon photonics send light along the absorbing layer instead of across it, so η can be high while the layer stays thin and fast. Coherent and balanced receivers use two matched photodiodes to cancel common noise; responsivity still sets the signal current in each. Datasheets quote responsivity at 1.31 µm and 1.55 µm along with dark current and bandwidth. Search next for "waveguide photodetector", "germanium-on-silicon photodiode" and "responsivity spectrum".

figure.caption: R = ηλ/1.24 rises with wavelength until the cutoff λ<sub>c</sub> = 1.24/E<sub>g</sub>, where it drops to zero. The dots are the two worked examples: silicon at 0.85 µm (0.548 A/W) and InGaAs at 1.55 µm (0.90 A/W); the dashed line is the η = 1 ceiling.
